source.title: Finite Versus Infinite Neural Networks: an Empirical Study
source.authors: Jaehoon Lee; S. Schoenholz; Jeffrey Pennington; Ben Adlam; Lechao Xiao; Roman Novak; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps network width and explicitly distinguishes its observed width behavior from double descent, reporting monotonic improvement in most settings and non-monotonic behavior in one setting that it says is not double-descent-like.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the width sweeps and their stated interpretation in §3.6 and Figure 6. The paper cites double-descent work as background, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. It does not report tests of error versus epochs or training-set size near an interpolation threshold; those omissions are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps width in finite FCN and CNN networks on CIFAR-10 (Fig. 6, S10). In §3.6 it argues that its width dependence is not captured by double descent. Every width tested is overparameterized, so the results bear only on the post-interpolation regime of V1 and V4, not on the peak.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that width usually improves performance monotonically. CNN-VEC with NTK parameterization has an intermediate optimal width; they call this non-monotonicity distinct from double descent because all widths are overparameterized. The abstract frames it as non-monotonic width dependence 'not captured by double descent phenomena.'
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps width in finite FCN and CNN architectures on CIFAR-10 and measures test accuracy. It does not reproduce the original double-descent sweep around the interpolation threshold or test epoch-wise and sample-size-wise curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Width behavior depends on architecture and parameterization: CNN-VEC with NTK parameterization is non-monotonic, unlike the stated monotonic-improvement cases.
record.problems: The width results are presented in Figure 6 without numerical values in the text; the paper does not identify an interpolation threshold for the width sweep. Test accuracy is used rather than test error.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant width outcomes were left out. Figure-only linearized/centered curves are not assigned separate result rows because the text does not describe their width trends, and the plots provide no extractable numeric values here.

untested.parts: The fall-rise-fall peak near the interpolation threshold: no width near the threshold is tested and none is identified.
Non-neural model classes; locating the interpolation point; the classical U-shaped regime.

missing.what: Width-by-L2 sweeps for widths 64–2048, including the finding that moderate widths benefit more from L2 under NTK parameterization. These bear on width dependence under regularization.
Separate standard-parameterization width panels and linearized/centered width curves; figure only, with no stated trends for the linearized curves.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' labels misread the design. The study never approaches the interpolation threshold, so the missing peak says nothing against V1. Monotonic improvement in the overparameterized regime matches the second descent. The only tension is r6, a large-width degradation that is a scope limit, not a refutation. All width evidence is figure only, with no numeric values. The authors note similar CNN-VEC behaviour reported in cited works [106, 107]; these are cited results, not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not identify a just-fitting/interpolation width or report a fall-rise-fall curve around it; reports test accuracy rather than test error.
No test of a fall-rise-fall test-error curve over training epochs.
No test of whether increasing training-set size near an interpolation threshold raises test error.
Tests width behavior in the studied neural-network architectures, not across non-neural model classes or generally across capacity measures; does not locate an interpolation point.
No unified effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
No test of label-noise-driven peaks, triple or multiple descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes such peaks.
No comparison against an effective parameter count to assess whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: FCN
rows.size_stated: Width varied; default FCN width is 2048
rows.stage_stated: Finite-width network trained with gradient descent
rows.operation_detail: Swept network width and measured test accuracy.
rows.measure: Test accuracy across width (the inverse direction of test error).
rows.note: The authors state that FCN performance improves monotonically with increasing width in both parameterizations in most cases; no double-descent peak is reported. The figure plots the listed training variants.
rows.check: The state was 'absent', but no peak is possible here: the authors say all widths are overparameterized. Monotonic improvement with width past interpolation matches the second descent V1 and V4 predict. Only that segment is tested; the peak is not.

rows.note: The authors report non-monotonic width dependence with an intermediate optimal width, but say this is distinct from double-descent-like behavior because all tested widths are overparameterized.
